title: Digital Life & Online Safety
description: Digital life and online safety from healthy screen habits to data rights: balancing screen time, asking a trusted adult, keeping personal information private, kindness online, how computers and the internet work, strong passwords, digital footprints, spotting misinformation, cybersecurity, recommendation algorithms, AI literacy, and privacy law and digital citizenship.

lessons.title: Screen Time and Green Time
objectives: Name healthy activities to balance screen time
Follow family rules about screens
explanation: Screens like tablets, phones and TVs can be fun and help us learn. But our bodies and brains also need running, building, drawing, reading and playing with people.
Health experts suggest young children have only a little screen time each day, with a grown-up, and lots of active play and sleep.
Screens off before bedtime helps us sleep well, because bright screens can make it harder to feel sleepy.

story.text: Ivaan loved his tablet games. One day, Mama set a sand timer. "When the sand runs out, we switch to green time." When the last grain fell, Ivaan groaned — then raced outside to look for snails. He found three! "Green time is good too," he admitted, holding up a snail.

lessons.title: Stop, Think, Ask
objectives: Name trusted adults to ask before going online
Tell a grown-up if something online feels scary or strange
explanation: Before going online, clicking on things or downloading games, always ask a trusted grown-up — like Mama, Papa, a grandparent or a teacher.
Sometimes pop-ups appear asking you to click or buy something. Don't click — show a grown-up.
If you see something that makes you feel scared, sad or confused, or someone you don't know talks to you, stop, close the screen and tell a grown-up. You will never be in trouble for telling.

lessons.title: Keep It Private
objectives: Identify personal information
Explain why personal information should stay private online
explanation: Personal information is information about you: your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday, passwords and photos.
We keep personal information private online, like keeping a treasure locked in a box. Only share it with a trusted grown-up's permission.
In games, use a nickname (username) that doesn't show your real name. Never share photos of yourself online without asking a grown-up.

story.text: Zuri's teacher gave each child a paper treasure box. "Put inside what you keep private online." Zuri drew her address, her school, her phone number and her password. On the outside she drew things that are okay to share, like her favourite colour. "Private things stay inside," she said, closing the lid.

lessons.title: Be Kind Online
objectives: Explain how to be kind online
Know what to do about unkind messages
explanation: There are real people behind every screen with real feelings. We should be as kind online as we are face to face.
Before sending a message, ask: Is it true? Is it kind? Is it helpful? If not, don't send it.
If someone sends unkind messages again and again, that is cyberbullying. Don't reply — tell a trusted adult, who can help block and report it.

lessons.title: Inside the Internet
objectives: Describe input, processing, output and storage
Explain that the internet is a network of connected computers
prerequisites: Can use a device with help
explanation: Computers take input (keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone), process it (with the processor, the "brain"), store it (memory and storage) and give output (screen, speakers, printer).
The internet is a giant network connecting billions of devices around the world. Information travels in small pieces called packets through cables — including undersea cables — and wireless signals.
Websites are stored on powerful computers called servers. When you visit a website, your device requests information from a server, and the server sends it back.

examples: Typing (input) and seeing words on screen (output).

story.title: The Packet's Journey
story.text: When Zuri sent a photo to her grandmother in London, the photo was split into thousands of tiny packets. They raced through Wi-Fi, along cables, under the ocean and through servers, each finding its own route. In London, they joined back together in the right order. Grandma saw the photo in seconds. "Magic!" she said. "Networks," said Zuri.

lessons.title: Make a Strong Password
objectives: Explain what makes a password strong
Create a memorable passphrase
explanation: A password is like a key to your account. A weak password like "123456" or "password" can be guessed in seconds.
Strong passwords are long and hard to guess. A good method is a passphrase — several random words joined together, like "PurpleMango!Rocket42". Longer is usually stronger.
Never share your password except with a trusted parent. Use different passwords for different accounts, so if one is found, the others stay safe.

vocabulary.meaning: a secret word or phrase to open an account
a password made of several words

examples: "TigerCloudBanana!7" as a passphrase.
"ivaan2020" as a weak password.

story.title: The Guessing Robot
story.text: Kiko's computer teacher showed a demo: a program tried common passwords. "123456" — cracked instantly! "kiko2015" — cracked in seconds. Then Kiko typed "JumpingRiver!Moon88". The program kept trying... and trying. "That would take a very long time," the teacher smiled. "Long and random wins."

lessons.title: Footprints That Don't Wash Away
objectives: Explain what a digital footprint is and why it lasts
Use privacy settings and think before posting
explanation: A digital footprint is the trail of information you leave online: posts, photos, comments, searches and even the websites you visit.
Things posted online can be copied, screenshotted and shared, so they may last for years — even if you delete them. Future schools or employers may see them.
Privacy settings control who can see what you share. Before posting, ask: Would I be okay with my grandparent, teacher or a future employer seeing this?

Meera apologised, and her classmate forgave her — but she learned that online, "delete" doesn't always mean gone.

lessons.title: Is It True?
objectives: Explain misinformation and why it spreads
Use simple checks to judge online information
explanation: Misinformation is false or misleading information. It spreads quickly because surprising or emotional stories get shared before people check them. Rumours forwarded in messaging groups have sometimes caused real harm.
To check information: Who made it? Is it from a reliable source (like a well-known news organisation, government or scientific body)? Do other reliable sources say the same? When was it published?
Images and videos can be edited or taken out of context. A reverse image search can show where a picture first appeared. When unsure, don't forward.

examples: An old flood photo shared as if it were new.

She checked a health ministry website and a trusted news site — nothing supported it. "Let's not forward it," Grandpa agreed. "Good detective work."

lessons.title: Spot the Phish
objectives: Identify signs of phishing and online scams
Explain multi-factor authentication, updates and backups
explanation: Phishing is when criminals pretend to be trusted organisations to trick you into giving passwords, OTPs or money. Signs include urgency ("Act now!"), unexpected prizes, spelling mistakes, strange sender addresses and links to look-alike websites.

Never share an OTP (one-time password) with anyone — banks will never ask for it. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second step, like a code on your phone, so a stolen password alone isn't enough.
Install software updates, which fix security holes, and back up important files. In India, cybercrime can be reported at cybercrime.gov.in or by calling the helpline 1930.

vocabulary.meaning: tricking people into revealing information by pretending to be trustworthy
a one-time password

examples: An SMS saying your bank account will be blocked unless you click a link.

story.title: The Urgent Message
story.text: Meera's aunt got a call: "This is your bank. Your card is blocked. Tell us the OTP we just sent to fix it." Meera remembered her cyber safety class. "Banks never ask for OTPs!" Her aunt hung up and called the bank directly using the number on her card. It had been a scam — and they had stopped it.

lessons.title: Why Your Feed Looks Like That
objectives: Explain how recommendation algorithms work
Evaluate filter bubbles and persuasive design
explanation: Apps use recommendation algorithms to choose what you see. They track what you watch, like, share and how long you look, then show more of what keeps you engaged.
This can create filter bubbles or echo chambers, where you mostly see views you already agree with. Content that provokes strong emotions often spreads furthest.

Persuasive design — infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications, streaks — is built to capture attention, because many platforms earn money from advertising time. Knowing this helps you take control: turn off autoplay, limit notifications and seek out different viewpoints.

vocabulary.meaning: rules a computer follows to make decisions

examples: Autoplay starting the next video automatically.

story.text: Kiko watched three cricket videos one evening. The next day, his feed was all cricket — highlights, arguments, angry rants about umpires. He realised he hadn't seen a single science video, which he used to love. He searched for some deliberately and turned off autoplay. "My feed, my choice," he decided.

lessons.title: Your Data, Your Rights
objectives: Explain how personal data is collected and used
Describe key rights under data protection laws
explanation: Companies collect data — location, contacts, browsing, purchases — to personalise services and target advertising. Combining data can create detailed profiles, raising concerns about surveillance, discrimination and data breaches.

India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires organisations to obtain consent for processing personal data for specified purposes, gives individuals rights to access, correct and erase their data, and requires verifiable parental consent for processing children's data. The European Union's GDPR (2018) is another influential law.
In 2017, the Supreme Court of India, in the Puttaswamy judgment, declared privacy a fundamental right under the Constitution.

examples: An app asking permission to access your location.

story.title: The Right to Privacy
story.text: Justice K. S. Puttaswamy, a retired judge, challenged the government over privacy concerns. In August 2017, a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right. The judgment shapes debates about data, surveillance and technology in India today.

lessons.title: Thinking Critically About AI
objectives: Explain how machine-learning systems are trained
Evaluate AI risks and practise responsible digital citizenship
explanation: Many AI systems use machine learning: they find patterns in large amounts of training data rather than following hand-written rules. Large language models predict likely text, which makes them fluent — but they can produce confident errors, sometimes called "hallucinations".

AI can reflect biases in its training data, for example performing worse for under-represented groups. Generative AI can create realistic deepfake images, audio and video, which can be used to deceive or harass. Checking sources and labelling AI-generated content matter more than ever.

Responsible digital citizenship means using technology ethically: respecting others' privacy and work, verifying before sharing, being honest about AI use in schoolwork, standing up against online abuse, and caring for digital wellbeing.
